eli10.body:
A MOSFET amplifier is a volume knob for electrical signals.

Imagine a stereo. You speak into a microphone — a tiny electrical signal. The amplifier boosts it, and the speaker blasts it out at full volume. The amplifier itself does not create energy — it uses power from the wall outlet to make a larger copy of your signal.

A MOSFET amplifier does the same thing. A small AC signal on the gate produces a much larger AC signal at the drain. The amplification factor is called the voltage gain A_v. It depends on two things: how sensitive the MOSFET is to gate voltage (transconductance g_m) and how much load resistance (R_D) converts the amplified current back to voltage.

More g_m or more R_D = more gain. But push too far and the output clips — like turning the volume knob past the speaker's limit.
eli10.pullquote: Small signal in, big signal out. That is the amplifier.

technical.body: The common-source (CS) configuration is the most basic MOSFET amplifier. The gate is the input, the drain is the output, and the source is the common (ground) terminal. The MOSFET must be biased in the saturation region (VDS > VGS − Vt) for amplification. A DC bias sets the operating point (Q-point), and the AC signal rides on top.

gm — transconductance = kn(VGS − Vt) = 2ID/(VGS − Vt). Units: mA/V or mS. Av — voltage gain = −gm × RD. Negative sign means the output is inverted. ro — output resistance = 1/(λ·ID). Finite ro means gain is actually −gm(RD ∥ ro). Vov — overdrive voltage = VGS − Vt. Larger Vov = more ID and gm.

More gain — increase gm (higher ID or wider W/L) or increase RD. More bandwidth — reduce parasitic capacitances (smaller transistor) or reduce RD. The trade-off — gain × bandwidth ≈ constant (gain-bandwidth product). You cannot maximize both. The A19 Pro's design team chooses the optimal point for each amplifier stage.

technical.h: GATE depth — what is actually tested
technical.body:
Voltage gain calculation A<sub>v</sub> = −g<sub>m</sub>R<sub>D</sub> (most common, 2-mark NAT). Transconductance g<sub>m</sub> = k<sub>n</sub>(V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>t</sub>). Q-point: find I<sub>D</sub> and V<sub>DS</sub> at the operating point. Small-signal equivalent circuit. Output resistance r<sub>o</sub> = 1/(λI<sub>D</sub>).

Multi-stage gain and source-degeneration appear as 2-mark problems.

realWorld.v: CS amplifiers in the DAC output stage — drive headphone signals from digital-to-analog
Amplifier stages before the ADC condition the signal — gain + anti-alias filtering
Accelerometer, gyro, magnetometer all need front-end amplifiers before digitization
The voltage-controlled oscillator uses tuned MOSFET amplifiers in a feedback loop
Higher g_m needs more I_D — more gain costs more power, always
Shorter channels → higher g_m per unit current → more gain-efficient amplifiers

lab.title: A19 Pro · audio codec amplifier
lab.brief: You are designing a common-source amplifier stage in the A19 Pro's audio codec. The microphone produces a 50 μV signal that must be amplified before the ADC. Your task: calculate the voltage gain |A_v| to verify the signal reaches the ADC's input range.
lab.hint: Find g_m = k_n(V_GS − V_t) first. Then |A_v| = g_m × R_D.

solution.line: I<sub>D</sub> = (k<sub>n</sub>/2)V<sub>ov</sub>² = (4/2)(0.16) = 0.32 mA. V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub> − I<sub>D</sub>R<sub>D</sub> — in saturation ✓
A 50 μV microphone signal becomes 400 μV after this stage — enough for the ADC input.

pyqs.q: A CS amplifier has k_n = 2 mA/V², V_GS = 0.9V, V_t = 0.5V, R_D = 10 kΩ. Find |A_v|. (2 dp)
pyqs.trap: Students sometimes use the wrong g_m formula. g_m = k_n(V_GS − V_t), not k_n·V_GS.

pyqs.q: Adding a source degeneration resistor R_S to a CS amplifier:
options: Decreases voltage gain but improves linearity
Converts it to a common-drain amplifier
pyqs.trap: Source degeneration introduces negative feedback: A_v = −g_m·R_D/(1+g_m·R_S). Gain decreases but bandwidth and linearity improve — a classic gain-bandwidth trade-off.

sol.line: R<sub>S</sub> introduces negative feedback. Gain drops by factor (1+g<sub>m</sub>R<sub>S</sub>) but linearity and bandwidth improve.

pyqs.q: A MOSFET in saturation has I_D = 0.5 mA and V_ov = 0.2V. Find g_m in mA/V. (2 dp)
pyqs.trap: Use g_m = 2I_D/V_ov = 2(0.5)/0.2 = 5.00 mA/V. Don't confuse with the BJT formula g_m = I_C/V_T.

pyqs.q: The output resistance r_o of a MOSFET in saturation is:
pyqs.trap: r_o = 1/(λ·I_D) = V_A/I_D. β/g_m is the BJT r_π formula — don't mix up.

sol.line: r<sub>o</sub> = 1/(λ·I<sub>D</sub>). Higher I<sub>D</sub> or larger λ → lower output resistance.

pyqs.q: A CS amp has g_m = 2 mA/V, R_D = 10 kΩ, r_o = 40 kΩ. Find |A_v| with r_o included. (2 dp)
pyqs.trap: A_v = g_m(R_D ∥ r_o) = 2 × (10×40)/(10+40) = 2 × 8 = 16.00. Students who ignore r_o get 20.

pyqs.q: In a common-source amplifier, the phase relationship between input and output is:
pyqs.trap: The negative sign in A_v = −g_m·R_D means 180° phase inversion. When V_in goes up, V_out goes down. This is the defining characteristic of the inverting amplifier.

sol.line: A<sub>v</sub> = −g<sub>m</sub>·R<sub>D</sub>. The minus sign → 180° phase inversion between input and output.

pyqInsight.body: MOSFET amplifier questions focus on g_m calculation and voltage gain. Source degeneration and output resistance appear as follow-ups.

practice.q: In a CS amplifier, doubling R_D while keeping the Q-point in saturation will:
options: Have no effect — gain depends only on g_m
Push the MOSFET into the triode region always
practice.why: |A_v| = g_m × R_D. Since g_m depends on the bias (V_GS, k_n), and R_D doubles, the gain doubles. But check: larger R_D means larger I_D × R_D drop, which may push V_DS below V_ov and into triode — the caveat.

practice.q: g_m = 3 mA/V, R_D = 4 kΩ, R_S = 1 kΩ. Find |A_v| with source degeneration. (2 dp)
k_n = 1 mA/V², V_GS = 1.0V, V_t = 0.5V. Find I_D in mA. (2 dp)
To increase g_m without changing I_D, you should:
options: Reduce the channel length below minimum
practice.why: g_m = √(2k_n·I_D) = √(2μ_nC_ox(W/L)·I_D). Increasing W/L raises k_n, which raises g_m for the same I_D. This is the fundamental sizing knob for analog designers.

practice.q: I_D = 0.25 mA, λ = 0.05 V⁻¹. Find r_o in kΩ. (2 dp)
